newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Russia defies NATO leader over troops in Moldova.
newsitem.headline: Russia defies NATO leader over troops in Moldova.

text.p: A Kremlin official, risking a new row with NATO, said on Tuesday Russia would pull troops out of Moldova's Dnestr region only when a political conflict there is resolved and not when the Western alliance demands.
Yuri Baturin, secretary of Russia's Defence Council, arrived in Moldova on Tuesday one day after NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana visited the former Soviet republic.

Russia has had troops based in Moldova's breakaway Dnestr region since clashes erupted over its independence moves in 1992, although Chisinau and Moscow signed an agreement for the troops to be withdrawn within three years.

"The OSCE Lisbon summit in December stated that the agreement reached in 1994 shall be complied with," Solana said during his visit to Moldova, referring to a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
Moldova's constitution does not allow the stationing of foreign troops on its territory.
But Baturin, whose country is already at odds with NATO over its plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe, hit back at Solana on his arrival in Moldova.
"So far, our troops are necessary here. We will act according to the situation, and not according to what Mr Solana says," he told reporters.
The withdrawal "will be synchronised to a settlement of the conflict in the region," Baturin said.

Leaders of Dnestr, whose independence claims have not been recognised abroad, have called for the 6,000 Russian troops to stay on. Clashes between the Dnestr rebels and Moldovan forces killed hundreds of people in 1992.
Moldova says it is ready to grant broad autonomy to Dnestr but not full independence.

Moldovan President Petru Lucinschi on Monday told Solana, who is touring ex-Soviet republics, that Moldova had no intention of joining NATO but would welcome security guarantees from the Western alliance.
Baturin, whose council is charged with overseeing military reforms, rejected the idea that only NATO, Moscow's old Cold War foe, should make such security guarantees.
"One should consider a system of security guarantees. We should talk not about guarantees only by NATO, but on behalf of all the influential participants of the European security process," he said.

Apparently responding to comments by another Kremlin official suggesting Moscow must reserve the right to use nuclear weapons if attacked with conventional arms, Baturin said Russia should not make threats with its nuclear arsenal.
"We should not threaten others with our nuclear armaments," Baturin said.
He said "it would be possible to resolve all problems without nuclear armaments, although Russia needs a nuclear shield".
